title: "Learning Rate"
description: "A parameter that controls the size of model-parameter updates during optimization."
term: "Learning Rate"
letter: "L"

## Simple explanation

The learning rate controls how big a step a model takes when adjusting its
parameters during training. If the steps are too large, training may jump
around or become unstable; if too small, learning can be very slow.

## Technical explanation

In gradient-based optimization, parameters $\theta$ are updated using the
gradient of a loss function. For a basic gradient descent step with learning
rate $\eta$:

$$
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla_\theta L(\theta_t)
$$

The learning rate scales the gradient-based update. Its useful value depends on
the model, data, optimizer, batch size, and training procedure.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

The learning rate is one of the most influential training settings. It affects
convergence speed and stability, and it often needs to be tuned or changed
during training. Large models may use a warmup period before reaching their
main learning rate.

## How it works

At each optimization step, the optimizer calculates an update from the loss
gradient and applies it to the parameters. A fixed learning rate uses the same
base scale throughout; an adaptive optimizer may additionally adjust effective
updates per parameter. A scheduler changes the learning rate over time.

## Practical example

When fine-tuning a pretrained image classifier, a modest learning rate helps
preserve useful learned features while adapting the model to new examples. A
rate that is too high can overwrite those features and make validation
performance worse.

## Common misconceptions

- A higher learning rate does not always make training finish sooner; unstable updates can prevent useful learning.
- The learning rate is not the same as the number of training examples or epochs.
- An optimizer's adaptive behavior does not make the learning-rate choice irrelevant.
